name: The Blank Wall On The Public Side
aka: the garage gable to the street
symptom: A wall facing a public street with no openings, or with one small obligatory bathroom window placed by the plan and not by the elevation. It is almost always a corner lot's side elevation, a garage flank, or the gable of a house turned to a side street, and it is finished in the cheapest cladding on the building with the trim reduced to corner boards. Somebody walking that street passes forty feet of nothing.

cause.explanation: One elevation on a production house is designed and three are generated. Windows on a side elevation cost $600-$1,400 each, add nothing to a listing photograph taken from the front, and complicate the interior layout, so a plan drawn for an interior lot puts closets, stairs, garages and bathrooms along its flanks. Dropped onto a corner lot, that flank becomes a public elevation and nothing in the process notices, because the elevation that was reviewed was the front one.
cause.cost_saved: $3,000-$8,000 in openings, trim and cladding upgrade on a 40 ft flank elevation.

rule_violated.statement: Where the house has two approaches it has two fully composed fronts. The two-front condition is a genuinely different building from the one-front condition and it is much more expensive, because the composition rules apply twice with no cheating on the back.

Every elevation facing a public street or a public open space is a front and is governed by the frontage standard, typically including a minimum transparency of 15 to 25 per cent for residential frontages.

rule_violated.ref: a street is made by the buildings that face it
rule_violated.statement: The public quality of a street is produced by openings: they supply the surveillance, the scale, the rhythm and the evidence of occupation. A blank wall does not merely fail to contribute; it actively removes those things from the length of frontage it occupies.

correct_practice: Any elevation visible from a public way is a front and is composed as one. The working standard: not less than 15 per cent of the street-facing wall area glazed for a residential elevation, with openings in a legible rhythm related to the principal front's - the same head datum, the same sill datum, the same or a subordinate opening proportion - and no run of blank wall longer than about 20 ft at ground level. Corner lots need the treatment carried around: the water table, the belt course, the frieze and the cornice all return the full depth of the flank, and the cladding does not change at the corner. Where a room genuinely has nothing to give - a garage, a stair, a store - the answer is either to give it a window anyway, which is what every historic urban building did, or to occupy the ground with something built: a garden wall with a gate, a loggia, a projecting bay, a pergola on the wall. What is not acceptable is a blank plane that changes material at the corner, because that announces which elevation was designed.

fixes.right: Compose the flank as a front: openings at the principal datums, at 15 per cent or more, with the trim assemblies returning the full depth.
fixes.cheap: Build the ground rather than the wall. A masonry or timber garden wall 5 to 7 ft high, returning from the flank to the side property line with a gate in it, costs $3,000-$8,000, screens the service yard, gives the side street an edge at human scale, and removes the blank wall from view without adding a single window. Where the wall is impossible, blind openings are legitimate and always were: a recessed panel with a proper sill, casing and head, at the same datums as the real windows, is a documented device on party-wall and fire-wall elevations and it reads correctly at forty feet.
fixes.dishonest: Painting on a pattern, applying shutters to blank wall, or fixing a false window unit with a mirrored or opaque insert. Shutters without an opening between them are the fault plus a second fault; a false sash unit is caught immediately by the absence of any reveal shadow and by the reflection, which is flat and dead where a real window reflects the sky and shows depth.

detection: Photograph the elevation square-on and measure glazed area against wall area. Below 10 per cent is the fault on a street-facing wall and below 5 per cent is severe. Second, look at the corner: a change of cladding, a stopped water table, a stopped cornice return or a change in trim width at the corner tells you the flank was not designed. Third, on a corner lot, compare the two elevations' opening datums - a flank whose window heads do not align with the front's has been laid out from the inside.

test.note: For an elevation facing a public street. 0.15 is the working standard and matches the transparency minima in most form-based residential frontage standards; the historic range for a secondary elevation is 0.10-0.18. This test must NOT be applied to the courtyard types, where the inverse rule holds - see inverted_by.

exceptions.why: The flank opposite the piazza sits at or within 3 ft of the property line and carries no more than token openings - it is a fire wall, a response to the Charleston fires of 1740 and 1778, and modern separation-distance rules reach the same answer.
exceptions.bounds: Blind flank only, on the north or east side, at or near the lot line. The STREET gable is not blind - it carries the false door and its two or three bays - and the piazza flank is fully open.

exceptions.why: The bermed uphill elevation has few or no openings by design because it is holding earth.
exceptions.bounds: Uphill wall only, below the principal floor, and only where the cross-slope is genuine at 1:8 or steeper.

exceptions.why: The end walls of a linear adobe range are commonly blind, because the openings serve rooms that run along the balcony side.
exceptions.bounds: End walls only; the long facade carries the balcony and its openings.

exceptions.why: Solid-to-void not less than 6:1 on principal elevations, with no opening wider than 6 ft; large glass belongs on courtyard-facing elevations only.
exceptions.bounds: The type's own ratio is about 0.14 void at most, so it sits right at the boundary. What is required is that the wall be modelled - stepped masses, canales, vigas, a portal - rather than a flat plane.

inverted_by.statement: The fault here is the opposite: a street elevation with domestic-scale windows in it. The type requires a blind or near-blind street wall with small, high, iron-grilled openings, one controlled entry through a zaguan, and all the light and life turned inward to the court. A picture window onto the street voids the type as decisively as a blank wall voids a Georgian corner.
Same inversion, and older: the outward-facing wall is a defensive and social boundary, and openings in it are the fault.

A monumental gateway in a wall that is otherwise entirely blank for a hundred metres is a named diagnostic tell. Punching windows into the casco wall destroys both the enclosure and the gate's authority.
The street wall is continuous and its openings are grilled and few; transparency standards written for Anglo-American frontages are simply the wrong instrument here.

In the courtyard variant the fault is an open street elevation: massing is organised around at least one outdoor room, ornament is concentrated at a single entrance against otherwise blank wall, and a minimum 12 ft run of unornamented wall each side of the entrance is required.

confused_with.difference: That is a change of MATERIAL at the corner. This is an absence of OPENINGS on the flank. They have the same driver - one designed elevation - and very often occur on the same wall, but each has its own fix.
That fault produces a single blinded bay in a rhythm; this is a whole elevation with no rhythm at all.

severity_by_style.why: A frontage standard applies to every street-facing elevation, and a blank flank on a corner lot defeats the block's whole premise.
On an end-of-row corner the flank is the most visible wall on the block.
Long low blank stretches on a side elevation are within the type's ordinary practice.
The type is at the boundary by its own solid-to-void rule; what matters is that the wall be modelled.
